title: Discovery Call: Brightwave Logistics

summary.overview: David and Marcus held a discovery call with Carla Mendes, operations director at Brightwave Logistics, a regional freight company with about 300 dispatchers and account managers. Brightwave loses details from carrier calls and customer escalations because nothing is recorded in a searchable form, and managers spend roughly six hours a week writing recaps. Carla's priorities are automatic action items, integration with their ticketing tool, and data residency in the US. A 60-day pilot with two teams was proposed, with a decision targeted for the end of next month once security review is complete.

transcript.summary: David and Marcus opened the call with Carla Mendes, operations director at Brightwave Logistics, a regional freight company of about 300 people across four offices. Carla said earlier recording tools only produced giant transcripts nobody read, so the bar is useful output.

points.text: Four Midwest offices; handoffs between offices are where information is lost.
points.at: handoff between offices is where information usually gets lost

points.text: Previous tools produced transcripts nobody read; Carla wants output that saves managers time.

transcript: Hi Carla, thanks for making time. I'm David, I lead our enterprise sales, and this is Marcus from our solutions engineering team. The plan is to spend about thirty minutes learning how your teams work today, and then we can talk about whether we're a fit.

Great, thanks for having me. I'm the operations director at Brightwave. We're a regional freight company, about three hundred people in dispatch and account management, working out of four offices across the Midwest.
Four offices is interesting. Are the teams in each office doing the same work, or is it split, for example dispatch in one place and account management in another?

It's mixed. Two offices are mostly dispatch, one is a hybrid, and the headquarters has account management plus finance. That matters because a handoff between offices is where information usually gets lost.
That's helpful. Before I ask questions, is there anything specific you wanted to get out of today so I make sure we cover it?

Mostly I want to understand whether this will genuinely save my managers time. We looked at a couple of recording tools last year and they just produced giant transcripts nobody read. I need something that produces useful output.
That is exactly the problem we try to solve, so I'm glad you raised it. Let's start with how a typical day looks for one of your dispatch teams.

transcript.summary: Dispatchers confirm pickup windows, rates and delays by phone all day, but the details live in notes or memory. A disputed detention fee cost about $4,000, and account managers spend roughly six hours a week on recaps.

points.text: Disputes are resolved by digging through emails and calling carriers, which strains the relationship.
points.at: Mostly emails and then phone calls

points.text: Phone recordings exist as unsearched files; video meetings have no record at all.
Halving recap time would return about 120 hours a week across the team.
points.at: a hundred and twenty hours a week

transcript: A dispatcher is on the phone with carriers all day. They confirm pickup windows, rates, and delays. Most of that lives in someone's notes or their memory, and when a customer escalates a week later we are reconstructing what was agreed.
How often does that reconstruction happen? Is that a weekly thing or more of an occasional problem?

At least a few times a week across the company. Last month we had a dispute over a detention fee where the carrier said we approved it on a call and we honestly could not prove otherwise. That one cost us about four thousand dollars.
Do you have a sense of how those disputes get resolved today? For example, does somebody dig through emails, or is it mostly he said, she said?
Mostly emails and then phone calls to try to jog people's memory. It's slow and honestly it damages the relationship with the carrier, because it feels like we're accusing them of lying.
That's a really concrete example. Are those calls already recorded in your phone system, or would this be a new capture?

Our phone system records some of them, but the recordings are just files in a folder. Nobody searches them. For team meetings and customer reviews, which happen on video calls, we have nothing at all.
Does the phone system have an export or an API? We could potentially ingest those call recordings too, so you wouldn't need agents to do anything differently for phone calls.
I believe it can export to cloud storage. That would be a stretch goal though. I'd rather prove the value on video calls first and then look at phone.
And what about the follow-up work after a customer review? Who writes the recap and sends the action items?

The account manager does. I asked a few of them to track it and the average was about six hours a week just writing recaps and updating tickets. Multiply that by the forty account managers and it's a lot of wasted time.
Six hours is significant. If we could cut that by even half, that's about a hundred and twenty hours a week back for your team.
Right, that is the number I would take to my CFO. The other piece is accountability. Action items get promised on calls and then forgotten, and customers notice.

Then let's make sure we give you something you can take to her. I can build a simple ROI sheet using your numbers, hours saved per week and the cost of a dispute, so the conversation isn't based on our claims.
Please do. She'll want to see the assumptions, so keep them transparent.

transcript.summary: Carla needs action items to become tickets without retyping, which Marcus said is possible through integrations and webhooks. Security requirements are US-only data residency and single sign-on, and Marcus will send the security whitepaper including retention details.

points.text: Video calls are a mix of Zoom and Teams; the ticketing system has a standard API.
points.at: Zoom and Teams depending on the customer

points.text: Data must stay in the United States and users must sign in with SSO.
points.at: single sign-on, because I will not manage

points.text: Retention is configurable; details will be included in the security package.

transcript: Let me ask about the technical side. Which tools do your teams use for tickets and for video calls, and where would you want the action items to end up?

We use a ticketing system for customer issues and our account managers live in it. Video calls are a mix of Zoom and Teams depending on the customer. Ideally an action item from a call becomes a ticket without anyone retyping it.

We can push action items out through an integration, and we have webhooks for custom workflows. A direct connector for your ticketing system depends on which one you use, but I'd expect it to be quick if it has a standard API.
It does have an API, but I'd have to involve my IT lead. He will care about security, so I should mention that up front.
That's good to know. What are the security requirements we should plan for?
Two big ones. Data has to stay in the United States because of a few customer contracts. And we need single sign-on, because I will not manage three hundred separate passwords.

Both are supported. Data residency in the US is a configuration option for your workspace, and single sign-on works with the common identity providers. I can send you our security whitepaper so your IT lead can review it ahead of time.
That would be great, and if it can include the details on how long you retain recordings, that will save me a round of questions later.
Yes, retention is configurable and I'll make sure that's in the package.

transcript.summary: David proposed a 60-day pilot with two teams (about 30 seats) priced per seat, with the cost credited toward an annual contract. Marcus offered to run a sample on anonymized recordings so dispatch jargon like deadhead and detention can be tested before the pilot starts.

points.text: Pilot priced at a discounted per-seat rate, credited if they move forward; no lock-in.
Success measured by recap time, completed action items and a manager survey.
A custom vocabulary can handle dispatch terms like deadhead, detention and lumper.

transcript: Let's talk about how to start. Rather than rolling out to all three hundred people, I'd suggest a sixty-day pilot with two teams, say one dispatch team and one account management team, so you can measure real results.
I like that. I don't want to commit the whole company on faith. How would you price a pilot?

For a pilot we usually price per seat at a discounted rate and credit it against the annual contract if you move forward. For about thirty seats I'd expect it to be well within a typical departmental budget. I'll put exact numbers in a written proposal.
And what happens at the end of the pilot, if we decide to expand? I don't want to be locked into a number that only works at thirty seats.

No lock-in. The pilot credit applies to the annual contract and the per-seat price steps down at volume tiers, so at three hundred seats it would be meaningfully lower. I'll show the tiers in the proposal.
That works. What would I be measuring to decide whether it succeeded?

I'd suggest three things. Time spent writing recaps, the percentage of action items that actually get completed, and a quick satisfaction survey from the managers. We can set the baseline in the first week.
Good, those are numbers I can defend. One more concern, though. Will it understand dispatch jargon? People say things like deadhead and detention and lumper all day.

Good question. We can add a custom vocabulary so those terms are recognized correctly. If you send me a few anonymized recordings, I can run a sample and show you how it handles your language before the pilot even begins.
I can do that. I'll need to scrub names and numbers first, but I can get you a handful of examples.
That's fine, and to be safe, anything you send will only be used for the sample run. We can delete it afterwards and send you written confirmation if your legal team wants it.
Yes please, legal will ask. If you can put that in an email I can forward it to them.

transcript.summary: David will send the proposal within three days and Marcus the security documents today. Carla will scrub and share sample recordings, and David will offer Thursday or Friday slots for a call with Brightwave's IT lead about the ticketing integration.

points.text: Proposal due within three days; security documents are sent today.
points.at: I'll send the pilot proposal within three days

points.text: Technical deep-dive with Carla's IT lead to be scheduled for Thursday or Friday of next week.
Security review must finish by the end of next month; a questionnaire can be turned around in days.
points.at: turn it around within a few days

transcript: Let me recap what I heard. I'll send the pilot proposal within three days. Marcus will send the security documents today. You'll share a few sample recordings, and then we'll set up a call with your IT lead about the ticketing integration.
That's right. When can we get that technical call on the calendar? My IT lead is busy but he's usually free late in the week.
I'll send a few options for Thursday and Friday of next week and you can pick whatever suits him. I'll book it once you confirm.
Perfect. And my goal is to decide by the end of next month, so we need security review done by then.
That's very doable. If your IT lead sends the questionnaire early, we can turn it around within a few days.
Thanks so much, Carla. This was really useful. I'll follow up with the proposal and the calendar options today.
